```{r setup-knitr, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

## Background

The `draw()` function combines plots of model terms into a single figure
using {patchwork}. Some terms need their own facets or coordinate systems,
so separate plots allow {gratia} to display them together.

Use ggplot2 themes to change the appearance of these plots. The `&` operator
applies a theme to every plot in the figure. This article shows how to style
{gratia} components and how to build plots from the underlying estimates when
you need different layers or mappings from variables to aesthetics.

## Adding layers to plots with the `&` operator

We start by simulating some data and fitting a GAM with four smooth functions

```{r setup-chunk}
library("gratia")
library("mgcv")
library("ggplot2")
library("dplyr")
library("patchwork")

# simulate data
n <- 400
eg1 <- data_sim("eg1", n = n, seed = 1)

# fit model
m <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3),
  data = eg1, method = "REML")
```

The default plot produced by `draw()` is

```{r draw-eg1-}
p <- draw(m)
p
```

If we want to change the theme for the plots, we can't append a `theme()` layer to `p` as this only affects the last plot in the *patchwork*^[A *patchwork* is the name given to the composition of individual plots created by `patchwork::wrap_plots()` or the composition operators `+`, `|` and `/`.]

```{r draw-eg1-wrong-theme}
p + theme_bw()
```

One way to apply the theme to all plots in the patchwork is to the the `&` operator.

```{r draw-eg1-right-theme}
p & theme_bw()
```

## Styling gratia components

Gratia uses ggplot2 themes for its plot components. Defaults retain the
existing appearance. Change an existing figure with `&` so every panel
receives the settings:

```{r native-component-theme}
p & theme(
  geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = "navy", linewidth = 0.8),
  geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = "navy"),
  gratia.alpha.interval = 0.15
)
```

Use `geom.gratia.partial.residual` for partial residuals,
`geom.gratia.diagnostic.point` for diagnostic points, and
`geom.gratia.reference` for reference lines. Opacity uses numeric settings
such as `gratia.alpha.interval` and `gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point`.
More specific settings, such as `geom.gratia.smooth.interval`, override
the general interval setting. See `?gratia_theme_get` for the component list.

Set a package override for subsequent plots without changing other ggplot2
plots. The override is attached when the plot is created:

```{r native-package-theme}
old_theme <- gratia_theme_set(theme(gratia.alpha.interval = 0.1))
draw(m)
gratia_theme_set(old_theme)
```

For temporary settings, use `withr::with_options()` with the option
`gratia.plot.theme`. Settings added to an existing plot follow normal
ggplot2 theme merging. Explicit deprecated aesthetic arguments remain fixed
overrides, even when they equal the old defaults. For example, replace
`draw(m, smooth_col = "navy", ci_alpha = 0.15)` with the component theme above.

Common replacements for deprecated arguments are:

| Previous argument | Theme setting |
|:--|:--|
| `smooth_col` | `geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `ci_col`, `ci_alpha` | `geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.interval` |
| `resid_col` | `geom.gratia.partial.residual = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `contour_col` | `geom.gratia.contour = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `point_col`, `point_alpha` in diagnostics | `geom.gratia.diagnostic.point = element_geom(colour = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point` |
| `line_col` in diagnostics | `geom.gratia.diagnostic.reference = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `colour`, `alpha` in smooth samples | `geom.gratia.sample = element_geom(colour = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.sample` |
| `ci_3d_col`, `ci_3d_alpha` | `geom.gratia.surface.interval = element_geom(fill = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.surface.interval` |
| `alpha`, `linewidth` in chain diagnostics | `gratia.alpha.chain`, `geom.gratia.chain = element_geom(linewidth = ...)` |

For parametric curves use `geom.gratia.effect`; for derivatives use
`geom.gratia.derivative`. Rootograms have separate `rootogram.bar`,
`rootogram.fitted`, `rootogram.reference` and `rootogram.warning` elements.
MRF interval lines use `geom.gratia.smooth.interval`, independently of the
points controlled by `geom.gratia.smooth`. Diagnostic boxplots use
`geom.gratia.diagnostic.boxplot`.

## Optional discrete palettes

Grouped curves and ribbons retain the current Okabe–Ito palette and hue
fallback unless another palette is requested. Use the same function for
colour and fill to keep groups paired:

```{r native-tol-palette}
tol <- gratia_palette("tol_banded_16")
theme(palette.colour.discrete = tol, palette.fill.discrete = tol)
```

Paul Tol choices include bright and vibrant (7 colours), muted (9),
dark (11), and banded schemes (12, 16 or 20). Dark favours visibility against
white; colours within larger banded schemes are less distinct. Finite
palettes error when their capacity is exceeded and do not interpolate or
recycle colours. See `?gratia_palette` for attribution and available names.

Continuous palettes can also be changed through
`palette.fill.continuous` and `palette.colour.continuous`. Existing scale
arguments still accept complete scales when custom transformations,
breaks or guides are needed.

## Combining individual plots produced by `draw()`

`draw()` methods like `draw.gam()` return an object created by `patchwork::wrap_plots()`, and as a result it isn't straightforward to combine those objects into a new patchwork

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks, error = TRUE, fig.show = "hide"}
p1 <- draw(m, select = "s(x0)")
p2 <- draw(m, select = "s(x1)")
p3 <- draw(m, select = "s(x2)")
p1 + p2 + p3
```

To avoid the error, we need to use `patchwork::plot_layout()` to set the dimensions we want

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks-layout}
p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

The above could have been achieved directly via `draw()`

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks-draw}
draw(m, select = c("s(x0)", "s(x1)", "s(x2)"), ncol = 3)
```

but it is instructive to know how to combine the outputs of `draw()` should the need arise, such as when you want to create a patchwork of plots from different models.

## Grouping factor smooths and showing their intervals

`grouped` selects which factor smooth types share a plot. Choose any of
`"factor-by"`, `"sz"`, and `"fs"`. Types omitted from the vector are drawn
separately for each level, or each evaluated combination of levels for `sz`
terms with several factors. `show_ci` independently selects which of these
types show interval ribbons. These controls apply to curves with one
continuous covariate; ordinary smooths and surface plots retain their displays.

The defaults, `grouped = c("sz", "fs")` and
`show_ci = c("factor-by", "sz")`, retain the existing grouping and interval
visibility. Use `character(0)` to select none. Here is a factor-by example:

```{r factor-plot-models}
factor_data <- data_sim("eg4", n = 400, seed = 244)
m_by <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2, by = fac), data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_sz <- gam(y ~ s(x2) + s(x2, fac, bs = "sz"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_fs <- gam(y ~ s(x2, fac, bs = "fs"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
```

Overlay the factor-by curves with intervals:

```{r factor-by-grouped}
draw(m_by, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)
```

Separate the `sz` deviations and hide their intervals. The ordinary smooth
retains its interval:

```{r sz-separate-no-intervals}
draw(m_sz, grouped = character(0), show_ci = "factor-by")
```

`fs` terms represent a fitted curve for each factor level. Separate those
curves and include their intervals with:

```{r fs-separate-intervals}
draw(m_fs, grouped = character(0), show_ci = "fs")
```

The same controls work with saved estimates. Changing their display does not
recalculate the estimates or interval bounds. Simultaneous bands keep their
coverage over the original fitted smooth, including its evaluated factor levels:

```{r factor-saved-estimates}
sz_estimates <- smooth_estimates(m_sz)
draw(sz_estimates, grouped = character(0), show_ci = character(0))
```

Ordered-factor `by` smooths use `"factor-by"` too. In the following model,
`s(x2)` is the reference smooth and the ordered-factor terms describe
deviations for the other levels. Grouping overlays only those deviations;
the reference smooth remains a separate plot. No smooth is created for the
ordered factor's first level, and the displayed deviations do not have the
reference smooth added to them.

```{r ordered-factor-grouping}
factor_data$ordered_fac <- ordered(factor_data$fac)
m_ordered <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2) + s(x2, by = ordered_fac),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
draw(m_ordered, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)
```

`grouped_by` is deprecated. Replace `grouped_by = TRUE` with
`grouped = c("factor-by", "sz", "fs")`; replace `grouped_by = FALSE` with
`grouped = c("sz", "fs")`. During migration, an explicit `grouped_by`
updates only `"factor-by"` membership in `grouped`.

## Drawing surfaces in 3D

Numeric smooth and parametric surfaces can be displayed with `surface = "3d"`.
The default remains `surface = "raster"`; `surface = "tile"` draws vector
rectangles. The 3D display retains the current diverging RdBu palette, fill
ranges, theme, and facet styling. Use `palette.fill.continuous` in `theme()`
to choose another palette.

```{r surface-3d, eval = requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)}
eg2 <- data_sim("eg2", n = 400, seed = 2)
m_surface <- gam(y ~ te(x, z, k = c(5, 5)) + x:z,
  data = eg2, method = "REML")
draw(m_surface, surface = "3d", n_2d = 20,
  surface_3d = list(yaw = 45, persp = FALSE))
```

`surface_3d` is a named list passed to `ggcube::coord_3d()`. gratia uses only the
coordinate system from that function, leaving its additional theme settings out.
Options such as `yaw`, `roll`, `pitch`, `persp`, `ratio`, and `light` configure a
shared view across all 3D panels. `surface_3d = list(dist = 3)` controls viewing
distance; the top-level `dist` argument still controls exclusion far from data.

Lighting defaults to `ggcube::light(backface_scale = 1)`, keeping the back faces
lit. Supply your own light object to replace this default, for example
`surface_3d = list(light = ggcube::light(backface_scale = -1))` to restore
ggcube's original back-face shading, or
`surface_3d = list(light = ggcube::light(method = "none"))` to disable lighting.
Surface faces have full opacity. Floor observations, boundaries, and contours
share the surface's depth ordering, so hidden parts are occluded by nearer faces.

For a different view for each term, customize the named plots from `assemble()`:

```{r surface-3d-per-term, eval = requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)}
panels <- assemble(m_surface, surface = "3d", n_2d = 20)
# coord_3d() returns a coordinate and a theme; take just the coordinate.
panels[["te(x,z)"]] <- panels[["te(x,z)"]] +
  ggcube::coord_3d(yaw = 45, persp = FALSE,
    light = ggcube::light(backface_scale = 1))[[1]]
panels[["x:z"]] <- panels[["x:z"]] +
  ggcube::coord_3d(yaw = -20, persp = FALSE,
    light = ggcube::light(backface_scale = 1))[[1]]
wrap_plots(panels)
```

The two displayed covariates form the horizontal axes, and the partial effect
forms the vertical axis. Higher-dimensional smooths and interactions retain
conditioning facets; `n_2d` controls surface resolution and `n_3d`/`n_4d` control
covariate slices. Contours follow the surface, and available observation locations
appear on the floor. No uncertainty surfaces are added. Direct calls to
`draw(smooth_estimates(model), surface = "3d")` and
`draw(parametric_effects(model), surface = "3d")` use the same renderer.

Scattered evaluation data use piecewise-linear Delaunay triangles and require
`geometry`. Support masking and soap-film domain checks also require
`sf`. Faces crossing known excluded regions are discarded conservatively; a
coarse mesh may therefore omit additional faces near a boundary. Increase the
evaluation density to resolve these areas. Spherical smooths retain their
geographic display.

## Building your own plot by hand

Themes control the appearance of plots returned by `draw()`. To choose
different layers or map additional variables to aesthetics, build a plot
from the estimates returned by {gratia}.

Instead, {gratia} also exports the lower-level functions used `draw()` so that you can create your own plot using whatever {ggplot2} functions make sense. In the next few code blocks we'll see how the plot created by `draw(m)` can be recreated by hand using these lower-level building blocks.

The main thing we need is to evaluate the smooths at values of their covariates. This is done using `smooth_estimates()`. We also need to add a credible interval to the evaluations, which can be done *tidyverse*-style via `add_confint()`

```{r custom-plot-eval-and-add-confint}
# evaluate the smooths
sm <- smooth_estimates(m) |>
  add_confint()
sm
```

By default `draw.gam()` will add partial residuals to the partial effects plots. To achieve the same effect, we need to add the partial residuals to the data used to fit the model. This can be done via `add_partial_residuals()`

```{r custom-plot-add-partial-resids}
# add partial residuals to data
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  add_partial_residuals(m)
```

This will^[currently; I'm not entirely happy with this naming convention as there's nothing to indicate to the user that these are *partial residuals* for the smooth with name matching the created variable name.] add columns with names `"s(x0)"`. `"s(x1)"`, etc. to the data.

```{r custom-plot-names}
names(eg1)
```

Now we have everything we need to recreate the plots created by `draw.gam()`. In the code block below we filter `sm` to focus on a specific smooth, here $f(x2)$ (`"s(x2)"`), then we add

1. a rug plot of the observed values of `x2`,
2. the credible interval around the estimated smooth,
3. the partial residuals as a point layer,
4. the estimated smooth as a line layer,
5. some annotation

```{r custom-plot-sx2}
p_sx2 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x2, y = `s(x2)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")
p_sx2
```


```{r custom-plot-other-smooths, echo = FALSE}
p_sx0 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x0)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x0),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x0),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x0, y = `s(x0)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x0, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x0)")

p_sx1 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x1)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x1),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x1),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x1, y = `s(x1)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x1)")

p_sx3 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x3)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x3),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x3),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x3, y = `s(x3)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x3, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x3)")
```

Assuming we repeat the above steps for the other smooths, creating plot objects `p_sx0`, `p_sx1`, `p_sx2`, and `p_sx3` (code not shown), we can complete the plot by creating the patchwork with the desired number of rows and columns

```{r custom-plot-final}
p_sx0 + p_sx1 + p_sx2 + p_sx3 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

The real benefit of having complete control over how the data are plotted is that you can use the power of {ggplot2} to map additional variables to plot aesthetics. As an example, let's assume we have a factor variable in the original data and we want to colour the partial residuals according to the levels of this factor. Let's create that factor

```{r add-factor-to-data}
set.seed(12)
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  mutate(fac = sample(letters[1:4], n(), replace = TRUE))
```

Now we can modify our plotting code to map `fac` to the colour aesthetic when we plot the partial residuals. To save some typing, we'll reorder the layers in the plot and add the partial residuals last

```{r plot-partial-resids-with-colours-by-fac}
plt <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")

plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = fac
    ), # <-- map fac to colour aesthetic
    data = eg1, size = 1.5
  )
```

We can also do some simple model checking by plotting the smooth with partial residuals coloured according to one of the other covariates (we could also do this by plotting the actual residuals against covariates). In the code chunk below, we map the covariate `x1` to both the *colour* and *size* aesthetics (note we deleted `size = 1.5` to allow the mapping to *size*)

```{r plot-partial-resids-with-colours-by-x1}
plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = x1, size = x1
    ), # <-- map fac to colour aesthetic
    data = eg1, alpha = 0.3
  ) + # <-- deleted cex!!
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma")
```

The resulting plot doesn't show any particular problems with the model because of the way the data were simulated, but hopefully this illustrates what can be possible once you use the low-level functions provided by {gratia}.
